name: Pre-workout / stim stacks

lead: Pre-workout stacks are powders, capsules and drinks taken before training, built mostly on caffeine and often paired with ingredients like beta-alanine, citrulline and creatine. The payoff lifters want is more energy and focus in the gym, which means harder, more frequent sessions and, over time, more muscle and a leaner build.

Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, which lowers perceived fatigue and pain. Other ingredients target blood flow and muscle buffering. Caffeine has research behind it for focus and endurance, results for many other ingredients are mixed, and commercial products often contain lower doses than the ones studied. No trials have looked at appearance outcomes.

paras: People take a serving before a session as part of a regular training routine, usually alongside a lifting program and a protein-rich diet. Products are sold as proprietary blends or as single-ingredient caffeine and creatine. The effect on energy and focus is felt within the session, while visible changes come from the training it supports over months.

Reported effects include raised blood pressure, nausea, jitters and sleep disruption when taken late in the day. Supplements have limited pre-market oversight in the US, and contaminated products and undeclared banned substances have been reported. People with heart or blood pressure conditions, or who are sensitive to stimulants, are usually advised to avoid high-stimulant products.

angle.text: Lifters take caffeine-based pre-workout blends to get more energy and focus in the gym, which lets them train harder and more often. Over months that training is what builds muscle and a leaner physique. Caffeine is the best-studied ingredient for performance; no trials have measured appearance.

lead: Pre-workout supplements are products taken shortly before training to raise energy, focus and endurance so that lifters can train harder and longer. They are sold as powders, capsules and drinks, and "stim stacks" are high-caffeine versions, or combinations of caffeine with other stimulants, favoured by people who want a noticeable push before a session [1]. The looks payoff runs through training: more intensity and volume across a program is what lifters say drives muscle gain and a leaner, more muscular physique.

Most products are proprietary blends averaging about 18 ingredients, with caffeine, creatine and beta-alanine in nearly all of them and caffeine in about 86 percent of best sellers in one study [1]. Other common components include citrulline and arginine for "pump", taurine, tyrosine, electrolytes and plant extracts [1].

Research on caffeine is substantial: the International Society of Sports Nutrition reports small to moderate acute benefits for muscular endurance, strength, sprinting and jumping, with aerobic endurance showing the most consistent effects [2]. A review of multi-ingredient pre-workouts reports positive effects on muscular endurance and mood, with mixed results for some other outcomes and with proprietary blends complicating comparison between formulas [3]. Reviews also describe cardiovascular and sleep effects of stimulant-heavy products [4][5].

paras: "Pre-workout" is a general term for bodybuilding supplements taken to improve endurance, energy and focus during training. Formulas vary by brand, and the category is lightly regulated [1]. Typical ingredients include caffeine and related stimulants (theophylline, theobromine), carbohydrates, electrolytes, nitric-oxide aids such as citrulline, arginine and beetroot nitrates, amino acids such as BCAAs, taurine and tyrosine, beta-alanine, and herbal extracts such as ginseng, ginkgo and rhodiola [1].

"Stim stack" usually means a high-stimulant combination, typically caffeine plus others such as theacrine, tyrosine or similar compounds. On looksmax.org, a member describes a product with 180 mg of caffeine as strong enough that users dance between sets [6]. On the T Nation forum, users review commercial pre-workouts, with one reporting a strong effect without jitters at one scoop and tingling at two [7], and older threads discuss timing of stimulant products and the warning labels against combining stimulants [8].

Dan Duchaine formulated Ultimate Orange in Venice, California in 1982, described as the first pre-workout and widely used by bodybuilders [1]. Ephedra-based stimulants linked with hypertension, stroke, seizure and heart attack were banned by the FDA in dietary supplements in 2004, creatine grew in popularity, and "pump" products with arginine and citrulline emerged in the early 2000s [1].

In 2005 chemist Patrick Arnold formulated a product containing DMAA, and Jack3d became a notorious high-potency brand linked to chest pain and heart risks before the FDA banned DMAA in 2012. Replacement stimulants such as DMBA, octodrine and DEPEA followed, and prohormones such as DHEA and CDMA were banned in 2014 [1]. The industry was valued at $2.7 billion in 2008 and $14.2 billion in 2022 [1].

The ISSN position stand reports that caffeine improves exercise performance in many but not all studies, with doses of about 3 to 6 mg per kg body mass shown to work consistently, a minimal effective dose possibly near 2 mg/kg, and side effects more frequent at very high doses (9 mg/kg) [2]. Caffeine acts as an adenosine receptor antagonist and is linked with better alertness and faster reaction time [1].

A cross-over trial compared a multi-ingredient pre-workout (beta-alanine, citrulline malate, arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, taurine, tyrosine, caffeine) with caffeine alone on bench press performance [9]. A 2025 randomised trial in middle-aged adults compared multi-ingredient pre-workouts with carbohydrate alone for resistance-training outcomes [10]. A randomised trial of citrulline malate found no improvement in muscle recovery after resistance exercise in untrained young men [11].

Wikipedia notes that reported energy effects are largely subjective, carbohydrate effects are inconsistent, and commercial doses of ingredients such as BCAAs and arginine are often below studied levels [1].

Beta-alanine causes temporary, dose-dependent tingling, and nausea and skin irritation are also reported. Caffeine can raise blood pressure, and higher doses may increase cardiac and liver risks; synephrine has been linked to heart problems [1]. A 2025 integrative review of 24 studies on pre-workouts and cardiovascular health reported possible cardiovascular changes classed as adverse or cardioprotective and described the literature as limited and conflicting [4]. A case report describes pancreatitis attributed to pre-workout use [12].

A meta-analysis of 24 studies found that caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and estimated that a standard pre-workout serving of 217.5 mg should be taken at least 13.2 hours before bedtime to avoid the reduction in total sleep time [5]. Sleep is also a recovery factor for muscle gain.

The FDA has minimal pre-market control over supplements, and quality studies report mislabelled contents. One study found melamine contamination in up to 50 percent of analysed pre-workout blends, and prohormones and SARMs are sometimes present undeclared, a frequent cause of failed athlete drug tests [1]. A review of selected food-supplement ingredients discusses risks of several common components [13].

Human studies cover caffeine [2], multi-ingredient pre-workout blends on bench press, basketball performance, anaerobic performance and resistance-training adaptation [9][10][14][15], theacrine [16], citrulline malate [11] and cardiovascular effects [4]. A review of multi-ingredient pre-workouts summarises positive effects on muscular endurance and mood, mixed effects on strength and power outcomes, and the difficulty of comparing proprietary blends [3]. No study has examined high-stimulant stacks as an appearance intervention.

lore.intro: Gym-focused forums discuss pre-workouts as a way to get energy and aggression for training, and members compare products and stimulant strengths [6][7][8].

claims.claim: High-caffeine pre-workouts produce a strong training boost.
Stimulants can be combined or stacked for greater effect.
Late-day pre-workout does not matter for recovery.

timeline.event: Dan Duchaine formulates Ultimate Orange, described as the first pre-workout [1].
FDA bans ephedra in US dietary supplements [1].
Patrick Arnold formulates a DMAA pre-workout; Jack3d follows [1].
Prohormones such as DHEA and CDMA are formally banned [1].
